title: QML for Quantum Sensing under Measurement-Induced Information Loss
abstract: Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond can serve as highly sensitive solid-state quantum sensors for high-sensitivity magnetometry. However, in the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era, extracting reliable information from noisy, finite-shot, and measurement-limited sensing data remains a considerable challenge. Whereas, quantum machine learning (QML) offers a potential path to improve parameter estimation by learning nonlinear relationships between quantum-sensing data and the underlying physical signal. In this work, we investigate the role of QML in magnetic-field estimation within an NV center-inspired magnetometry setting. We formulated magnetic field sensing as a supervised regression task. We compared the performance of several classical machine learning models trained on measurement-based classical data with that of quantum kernel-based models trained on pre-measurement coherent quantum states. Our objective is to isolate the impact of measurement-induced information loss and therefore provide a theoretical upper bound on the sensing performance. The upper bound is achievable only when coherent quantum information is directly available to the learning model. Our results show that QML-based sensing performance improves significantly with coherent quantum-state information, and not much with changes in model complexity or learning paradigm. This observation underscores the importance of learning pipelines that tightly integrate quantum sensors and QML models to enhance magnetic field sensing under realistic constraints.
summary: This work investigates how Quantum Machine Learning (QML) can enhance magnetic field sensing using NV centers, focusing on the impact of measurement noise. By comparing models trained on raw measurement data versus those using pre-measurement quantum states, the authors show that access to quantum coherence provides a substantial, theoretically achievable performance boost. This underscores the need for quantum-native learning pipelines to minimize information loss in real-world quantum sensors.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of extracting reliable parameters from noisy, measurement-limited quantum sensing data in the NISQ era.
main_result: QML-based sensing performance significantly improves when utilizing pre-measurement coherent quantum-state information, demonstrating that measurement-induced information loss is the primary bottleneck.
method: The authors formulated magnetic field estimation as a supervised regression task, comparing classical ML models trained on measurement statistics against quantum kernel models trained on coherent quantum states.
model_or_system: The study uses a Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center in diamond as a quantum sensor, simulating Ramsey interferometry governed by a Zeeman Hamiltonian. The process involves unitary evolution followed by projective measurement.
key_observables: Magnetic field ($B$), estimation error (RMSE), and the comparison between classical vs. quantum kernel model performance.
important_parameters: Magnetic field range ($B \in [0, 2] \mu T$), evolution times ($\{5, 10, 20, 40, 60\} \mu s$), and noise parameters like $T_2$ and readout error.
main_assumptions: The core comparison assumes that classical models are limited by measurement statistics, while quantum models can access the theoretical upper bound provided by coherent states.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the NV center level diagram, the Ramsey interferometry setup, and comparative plots showing the gap between the theoretical upper bound (coherent state access) and measurement-limited model performance.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the sensing problem using NV centers, details the data acquisition by comparing classical (measurement-based) and quantum (coherent state) data types, and concludes by quantifying the performance gap attributable to measurement-induced information loss.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, quantitative framework for understanding the limitations imposed by measurement back-action on quantum sensing protocols, which is crucial for designing fault-tolerant quantum measurements.

Without any external magnetic field, the energies of the orbital ground states, ∈{|0⟩, |±1⟩}, split, called zero field splitting (ZFS). In the presence of an external magnetic field, BNV along the quantization axis of the crystal, the degenerate ground states, |+1⟩and |−1⟩, split up, which is referred to as Zeeman splitting.
